actions.name: Review clinic referral note
actions.result: Referral from primary care clinic: patient referred to CHW outreach after missing 3 consecutive appointments (last visit no-show x3 over 4 months). Most recent HbA1c 10.2% (prior value 8.9% about 6 months ago). PCP requests outreach to assess barriers to care and support re-engagement.

actions.name: Review medication list in chart
actions.result: Insulin glargine 20 units subcutaneous nightly; Metformin 1000 mg oral twice daily; Lisinopril 10 mg oral daily. Pharmacy fill history shows glargine pen last filled 54 days ago (30-day supply); no refill request since.

actions.name: Review last clinic vitals and labs
actions.result: Last in-clinic visit 7 months ago: BP 138/84, weight 192 lb. HbA1c trend: 7.8% (14 months ago) -> 8.9% (7 months ago) -> 10.2% (drawn 2 weeks ago via outreach lab draw).

actions.name: Administer standardized social needs screening (food, housing, transport, utilities, cost of care)
actions.result: Positive screens: food insecurity (runs out of food/money for food in the last 12 months - sometimes true), transportation barriers to medical care, cost-related medication underuse. Negative screens: housing is stable (owns home with family), utilities not shut off, no interpersonal safety concerns reported.

actions.name: Visual inspection of feet via camera (patient self-exam, CHW-guided)
actions.result: Patient holds both feet up to camera one at a time. No visible open wounds, redness, or swelling noted on either foot by camera; skin appears intact. CHW notes this is not a substitute for a clinical foot exam and recommends one be scheduled.

actions.name: Screen for mood and emotional wellbeing
actions.result: Patient denies feeling down most days, denies thoughts of self-harm. Describes feeling tired and occasionally overwhelmed by juggling family responsibilities and health needs but does not endorse symptoms consistent with depression on brief screen.

actions.name: Document encounter and relay concerns to care team
actions.result: Outreach note completed and routed to PCP/care team flagging: insulin dose rationing due to cost, 4-week gap in glucose test strips, new nocturnal bilateral foot tingling/burning, transportation and food insecurity barriers, and patient-identified goals. Recommends clinical review of insulin regimen/affordability and a diabetic foot exam; CHW does not alter medication regimen.

actions.name: Review community resource directory for local food assistance
actions.result: Local food pantry (weekly distribution, no documentation required) and a mobile grocery voucher program for residents with diabetes are available in Springdale; both accept walk-in enrollment.

actions.name: Review patient assistance program options for insulin cost
actions.result: Manufacturer patient assistance program and a local Rx assistance fund both list eligibility for uninsured/underinsured residents; application requires proof of income and a prescription from the prescribing clinic - CHW can assist with paperwork but cannot adjust the prescription.

profile.encounterType: Social needs screening and health coaching visit

facts.chart: Patient referred to CHW after missing 3 clinic appointments; recent HbA1c 10.2%.
facts.says: They told me I need to talk to someone because I missed some appointments and my sugar numbers aren't good.

facts.chart: Diagnosed with type 2 diabetes approximately 8 years ago.
facts.says: I've had the sugar for about eight years now.

facts.chart: Reports clinic hours conflict with weekday childcare duties.
facts.says: The clinic is only open when I'm watching my grandkids, so it's hard to go.

facts.chart: Cares for three grandchildren (ages 4, 7, 9) weekdays 7am-5pm while daughter works.
facts.says: I have my grandbabies every weekday, the little ones, while my daughter's at the factory.

facts.chart: No personal vehicle; relies on public bus with two transfers, 70-90 minutes each way to clinic.
facts.says: I have to take the bus and change twice, it takes almost an hour and a half just to get there.

facts.chart: Reports food budget runs out before end of month; relies on food pantry items.
facts.says: By the end of the month the money's tight, so we eat a lot of tortillas and rice and whatever the pantry gives us.

facts.chart: Food pantry provides mostly canned and boxed goods.
facts.says: The pantry food is mostly cans and boxes, not always the freshest things, but it helps.

facts.chart: Patient states she takes insulin as prescribed because she does not want to be scolded by the clinic.
facts.says: I tell them I take it just like the doctor said, I don't want them getting on me about it.

facts.chart: Discloses she sometimes takes half her prescribed insulin dose when money is tight to stretch the supply.
facts.says: Sometimes when things are tight I only take half, just so it lasts till I can get more.

facts.chart: Reports cost of insulin copay as the reason for dose reduction, not confusion about instructions.
facts.says: It's not that I forget, it's just the money, the pen costs more than I have some months.

facts.chart: Has Medicaid coverage; reports approximately $35/month copay for insulin.
facts.says: I have the state insurance but I still pay around $35 for the insulin pen most months.

facts.chart: Out of glucose test strips for approximately 4 weeks; has not checked blood sugar at home.
facts.says: I haven't had the little strips for about a month now, so I haven't checked my sugar at home.

facts.chart: Reports nightly bilateral burning/tingling in feet for several months.
facts.says: My feet tingle and burn at night, both of them, it's been like that for a few months.

facts.chart: Denies any foot wounds, sores, or injuries.
facts.says: No, I don't have any cuts or sores on my feet, I check sometimes.

facts.chart: Denies color changes or swelling in feet.
facts.says: They don't look different in color or anything, no swelling.

facts.chart: Owns her home; lives with extended family; reports housing as stable.
facts.says: We own our little house, it's just me and sometimes my daughter's family stays too, it's crowded but it's ours.

facts.chart: Denies any utility shutoffs or threats of shutoff.
facts.says: No, the lights and water are fine, we keep up with those.

facts.chart: Denies persistent low mood; describes feeling tired and occasionally overwhelmed.
facts.says: I get tired and sometimes it feels like a lot, but I'm not sad all the time or anything like that.

facts.chart: Denies thoughts of self-harm.
facts.says: No, nothing like that, I would never think that way.

facts.chart: Former poultry-plant worker; retired/left due to physical demands of the job.
facts.says: I worked at the chicken plant for over twenty years before my body couldn't keep up with it anymore.

facts.chart: Daughter and grandchildren live nearby; daughter works full-time at a factory.
facts.says: My daughter works at a factory, long hours, that's why I have the kids during the day.

facts.chart: Walks with a neighbor several times a week when schedule allows.
facts.says: When I can, my neighbor and I walk together, maybe a few times a week.

facts.chart: States wanting to 'get back on track' with blood sugar and find affordable way to attend appointments without disrupting daughter's work.
facts.says: I just want to get back on track with my sugar, and find a way to go to my appointments without messing up my daughter's work.

facts.chart: Identifies walking with neighbor and simplifying pantry-food meals as changes she is willing to try.
facts.says: I think I could keep walking with my neighbor, and maybe figure out better ways to cook what the pantry gives us.

facts.chart: Reports enjoying cooking; expresses interest in healthier recipes using accessible ingredients.
facts.says: I love to cook, I just wish I knew better ways to make it healthy with what we have.

facts.chart: Expresses fear of being judged or scolded by clinic staff about medication use.
facts.says: I just don't want them to think I'm not trying, because I am trying.

facts.chart: Bilingual Spanish/English; more comfortable with simple English in conversation.
facts.says: I speak some English, simple words are easier for me, but I understand a good amount.

facts.chart: Mentions neighbor's dog as a reason walks sometimes get skipped.
facts.says: Sometimes we skip the walk because her dog isn't feeling well and she stays home with him.

facts.chart: Has a son living out of state who she speaks with by phone weekly.
facts.says: My son lives in Texas, we talk on the phone most weeks.

facts.chart: Diagnosed with hypertension approximately 5 years ago, on lisinopril.
facts.says: I have the high blood pressure too, been on that pill for a few years.

facts.chart: Reports taking metformin and lisinopril as prescribed without interruption, no cost barrier reported for these.
facts.says: The other two pills I take fine, those aren't as expensive.

facts.chart: Not currently employed outside the home; left poultry plant job due to physical strain and now provides unpaid caregiving.
facts.says: I don't work outside anymore, taking care of the grandkids is my job now, really.

artifacts.title: Primary Care Referral to Community Health Worker Outreach
artifacts.author: Dr. Alvarez, Springdale Community Health Clinic
artifacts.body: Patient referred for CHW outreach after 3 consecutive missed appointments over the past 4 months. Last contact by phone was reassuring regarding medication adherence, but recent labs show significant worsening of glycemic control. Requesting assessment of barriers to care (transportation, scheduling, cost) and support for re-engagement with the clinic. Please report any safety concerns, including neuropathy symptoms, medication-taking concerns, or acute needs, back to care team promptly.

artifacts.title: Social Needs Screening Results
artifacts.author: CHW Outreach Program
artifacts.body: Food insecurity: Positive (sometimes true to statement 'food didn't last and there wasn't money to get more' in past 12 months). Housing stability: Negative (stable homeownership). Transportation barriers to care: Positive. Utility security: Negative. Interpersonal safety: Negative. Cost-related medication underuse: Positive (see outreach note for detail).

artifacts.title: Prior Clinic Visit Note (7 months ago)
artifacts.author: Dr. Alvarez, Springdale Community Health Clinic
artifacts.body: 61-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension presents for routine follow-up. BP 138/84, weight 192 lb. HbA1c 8.9%, up from 7.8% at prior visit. Patient reports taking insulin glargine and metformin as prescribed with no barriers noted. Advised continued adherence and lifestyle modification. Follow-up in 3 months recommended; patient did not return until outreach referral generated after repeated no-shows.

objectives.text: Build rapport and trust sufficient to elicit sensitive disclosure of cost-driven insulin dose reduction and the patient's reasons for underreporting it to the clinic, recognizing patients may underreport nonadherence to avoid judgment.
Conduct a structured social needs screen covering food, housing, transportation, utilities, and cost of care, correctly distinguishing positive from negative domains.
Identify and relay to the care team red-flag findings outside CHW scope (insulin rationing, gap in glucose monitoring, new neuropathy symptoms) without attempting to diagnose or adjust medications.
Elicit the patient's own goals in her own words and negotiate one or two patient-chosen, achievable behavior-change goals rather than imposing clinician-driven targets.
Connect the patient to concrete community resources (food pantry, transportation options, medication assistance programs) matched to the specific barriers identified.
Recognize and gently explore a mismatch between what the patient reports to the clinic and what the chart/record shows, without shaming the patient.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient tells the clinic she takes her insulin exactly as prescribed, out of fear of being scolded.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Prior clinic note documents patient reported taking insulin and metformin as prescribed with no barriers, 7 months ago, while HbA1c has since risen sharply to 10.2% and pharmacy fill history shows a 24-day overdue refill.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Patients may underreport nonadherence to clinicians due to fear of judgment; a trusted CHW relationship in a different context can surface the true barrier (cost-driven dose rationing) that the clinical record alone would not reveal.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient says she sometimes takes only half her insulin dose to stretch the supply when money is tight.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Pharmacy fill history shows the glargine pen was last filled 54 days ago for a 30-day supply, consistent with the patient stretching a one-month supply to cover roughly two months.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Objective pharmacy refill timing can corroborate a patient's self-report of dose rationing, supporting the CHW's role in validating and relaying concerns to the clinical team.

patient.name: Guadalupe "Lupe" Mendoza
patient.occupation: Former poultry-plant worker; currently unpaid family caregiver
patient.appearance: A woman with graying dark hair pulled back, wearing a floral apron over a t-shirt, seated at a kitchen table with a child's crayon drawings taped to the wall behind her. Her affect is warm and a little tired, with a ready smile that fades when sensitive topics come up, and she occasionally glances off-camera toward sounds of children playing in another room.

persona.personality: Warm, humble, self-effacing, puts family and others' needs before her own; takes pride in being capable and not wanting to be a burden.
persona.communicationStyle: Speaks in simple, friendly English with occasional Spanish phrases; tends to minimize her own struggles and redirect concern toward her grandchildren or daughter; needs gentle, repeated invitation before disclosing sensitive details.
persona.emotionalState: Mildly anxious about being judged, tired, but hopeful if treated with respect and without blame.
persona.background: Worked over two decades at a regional poultry processing plant before physical strain forced her to stop. Now provides full weekday childcare for her three grandchildren while her daughter works a factory shift. Enjoys cooking traditional family recipes and takes pride in keeping her household running despite tight finances.
speechExamples: I don't want to be any trouble, I know you're busy.
My grandkids keep me young, even when I'm tired.
I try to do what the doctor says, I really do try.
It's not a big deal, I manage, I always manage somehow.
I just want to get back on track, that's all.
concerns: Being judged or scolded by the clinic for not managing her diabetes well
Missing time that would affect her daughter's work schedule or childcare arrangements
Affording her insulin and getting to appointments
Whether the tingling in her feet means something serious is wrong

scenario.studentBrief: You are a community health worker conducting a telehealth outreach visit with Lupe Mendoza, 61, referred by her primary care clinic after missing recent appointments. Your role is to build trust, screen for social needs, support her in setting her own goals, connect her to resources, and relay any clinical concerns to her care team. You do not diagnose conditions or give medication instructions.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Referred for missed appointments and poor diabetes control; patient reports feeling behind on managing her health.
scenario.openingLine: Hi, thank you for calling me back. I know I've missed a few appointments at the clinic, and they said my sugar numbers aren't good right now.
tasks: Build rapport and conduct a social needs screen covering food, housing, transportation, and cost of care
Explore barriers behind the missed appointments with curiosity rather than judgment
Identify any safety concerns (medication-related or symptom-related) that need to go back to the care team
Collaborate with the patient to set one or two goals in her own words
Identify and offer at least one concrete community resource matched to an identified barrier

answerKey.primaryProblem: Poorly controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 10.2%) driven by social and financial barriers, including cost-related insulin dose rationing, a month-long gap in glucose test strips, food insecurity, and transportation barriers to clinic appointments; new report of bilateral nocturnal foot burning/tingling concerning for peripheral neuropathy requiring clinical evaluation.
differential: Cost-related insulin underdosing as primary driver of hyperglycemia (most likely given disclosed dose reduction and overdue refill pattern)
Diabetic peripheral neuropathy (new bilateral nocturnal foot symptoms, requires clinical/diagnostic evaluation - outside CHW scope to diagnose)
Suboptimal glycemic control from dietary pattern changes related to food insecurity (contributing factor, not sole cause)
Missed appointments due to logistical/scheduling barriers rather than disengagement from care
keyFindings: HbA1c rose from 7.8% to 8.9% to 10.2% over 14 months
Pharmacy fill history shows insulin glargine refill 24 days overdue, consistent with dose stretching
Patient discloses taking half her prescribed insulin dose when funds are tight
No glucose test strips for approximately 4 weeks; no home monitoring during that time
New bilateral nocturnal foot burning/tingling for several months, no wounds or color change on camera inspection
Food insecurity and transportation barriers (two bus transfers, 70-90 minutes each way) both screen positive
Patient tells clinic she takes insulin as prescribed, differing from what she discloses to the CHW, out of fear of being judged
plan: Relay to care team (PCP/clinical pharmacist/diabetes educator): insulin dose rationing due to cost, gap in test strips, and new neuropathy symptoms for clinical evaluation and possible regimen/affordability review - CHW does not adjust medications or diagnose neuropathy
Assist patient with application to insulin manufacturer patient assistance program or local Rx assistance fund to address copay burden
Connect patient to local food pantry and mobile grocery voucher program for diabetes-appropriate food access
Explore transportation solutions: ask clinic about telehealth follow-up options, medical transport benefit through Medicaid, or appointment scheduling outside caregiving hours
Document and support patient-chosen goals: continuing walks with neighbor and exploring healthier recipes using available pantry foods
Schedule or encourage follow-up clinical visit (in person or telehealth) for diabetic foot exam and glycemic management review
Approach adherence conversation nonjudgmentally in future encounters to maintain trust and encourage honest disclosure to the full care team
redFlags: Insulin dose rationing due to cost with markedly elevated HbA1c (10.2%) - risk of worsening hyperglycemia or complications
New bilateral nocturnal foot burning/tingling - possible peripheral neuropathy requiring timely clinical evaluation
No home glucose monitoring for about a month in setting of poor control - limits ability to detect dangerous highs or lows
educationPoints: Patients may tell clinicians what they think will avoid judgment; a CHW's trust-based relationship can surface true barriers like cost-driven medication rationing
Social needs screening should cover food, housing, transportation, utilities, and cost of care as distinct, specific domains
CHWs support patient-defined, achievable goals rather than imposing clinical targets, which improves engagement and follow-through
Clear role boundaries matter: CHWs identify and relay concerning symptoms or medication-related safety issues to the clinical team rather than diagnosing or advising on treatment
Pharmacy refill timing can be a useful objective corroborator of patient-reported medication-taking patterns

profile.title: Social Needs Screening and Health Coaching: Cost-Related Insulin Rationing in a Caregiver with Rising HbA1c
profile.summary: Lupe Mendoza, 61, is referred to a community health worker after missing three clinic appointments with her HbA1c rising to 10.2%. The case teaches trust-based disclosure of cost-driven insulin dose rationing, structured social needs screening, patient-centered goal setting, and appropriate escalation of medication and neuropathy concerns to the care team within CHW scope of practice.
profile.setting: Telehealth video visit, patient at home in her kitchen in Springdale, Arkansas
